newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGOLUX STEEL SHARES OUTPERFORM IN BRUSSELS.
newsitem.headline: BELGOLUX STEEL SHARES OUTPERFORM IN BRUSSELS.

text.p: Belgian steel group Cockerill Sambre held up well on a weak Brussels bourse on Tuesday, buoyed by the prospect of German capacity cuts after news of Krupp's planned takeover of Thyssen AG , analysts said.
"There's still overcapacity in the steel market in Europe so if capacity is cut with this deal that's favourable for the steel market as a whole," said Patrick Gelderman at Kredietbank.
Cockerill shares ended the day just one franc lower at 124 after peaking at 126, while Luxembourg steelmaker Arbed ended 20 francs higher at 3,670.
"A Krupps-Thyssen merger would pull out some capacity, which is good. But in the end only competitive companies will survive," added Corluy analyst Kristoff Van Houte.
If Krupp's hostile takeover bid succeeds it will create one of the world's largest steel and engineering conglomerates, and could spark further European steel industry consolidation.
However Belgian analysts were sceptical when asked about the possibility of a Cockerill-Arbed merger in the future.
"It is unlikely because Cockerill is principally state owned and considering the difficulties on the labour front (a merger would cause), it would never pass," Van Houte said.
"A merger between Cockerill and Arbed is unlikely - certainly in the short term," Geldermans said. "It's a problem of the political agenda of the Walloon Region.

Cockerill is almost 80 percent owned by the Walloon Region's steel investment company, though is essentially run as a private company. Recognising itself as a smallish player on a European scale it has not ruled out the possibility of a future alliance if a suitable industrial partner could be found.
Together with its German unit EKO Stahl it produced 6.3 million tonnes of raw steel in 1995. By comparison Arbed produced 11.5 million tonnes.
"Arbed, I guess, can make it on its own," Van Houte added.

Attempts last year by the Walloon Region to involve Cockerill in a rescue plan for the small, bankrupt Walloon steel firm Forges de Clabecq SA failed because Cockerill said there was a lack of synergies between the two. The Walloon Region was also Clabecq's biggest shareholder and creditor.
Cockerill also abandoned talks last December with privately-owned Belgian steel firm Usines Gustaves Boel, which later signed a merger with Dutch steel group Hoogovens.
